newsitem.title: INDIA: Buba's Gaddum says future favours the mark.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Gaddum says future favours the mark.

text.p: Bundesbank Vice President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said on Monday he saw no reason for a weaker mark while the German currency floundered near 34-month lows against the dollar.

Speaking to Reuters in Bombay, he said he understood why investors were attracted by the dollar at present, but did not believe the currency markets were seeing the full picture of future expectations.
"There is no reason for a weaker deutschemark," he said after delivering a speech to the Indo-German Chamber of Commerce.
"I am not looking for strength for the dollar, I am looking for the strength, possible future strength of the deutschemark," he said.
The dollar struck a 34-month high of 1.6962 marks in Asian markets on Monday, but in early European trade the dollar had slipped slightly to around 1.6930.
Earlier this month the Group of Seven (G7) nations reached a consensus in Berlin that the surging dollar had risen far enough.
Gaddum said he understood why investors were drawn to the dollar by a U.S. economy showing good inflation and employment performances and a booming stock market.
"I can understand now that the dollar is a currency they like to invest (in)," Gaddum said.
But he said there were future expectations that favoured the mark more than the market appreciated.
"I would say that expectations for the deutschemark are better than the market is seeing at the moment," he said.
"I would not say they (the foreign exchange markets) are looking at the wrong things but maybe they see, not completely, the right things," Gaddum said.
"They must see that the situation in Germany is at the moment very difficult. The headlines of the newspapers are influenced by the very high unemployment rate. That is one of our problems," he said.
The Bundesbank official then listed other factors showing positive influences.
"The productivity of companies in Germany is much better than we had three or four years ago. Second, we have extremely low capital market rates, we have an all-time low in money market rates.
"If you see the development of the exchange, this reflects the situation in companies. We have a steady growth of our exports. Therefore there are a lot of positive factors in the German market."

Gaddum said German industry was being challenged by low wage European countries, particularly in eastern Europe, but German companies were investing in these countries and Germany would eventually reap the benefits.

"One of the problems we have is the competition situation between Germany and especially eastern Europe at the moment, because in those areas they have lower wages," he said, adding German companies were more interested in investing in these countries than in Germany.
"If you see the fundamentals of the future they are encouraging for the deutschemark," he said.
Gaddum was asked which way German interest rates were likely to move next, but refused to be drawn.
"That is difficult to say... but you can be sure that if it is necessary to act we can act in each direction," he said.
